div.head: Hl 15
div.ab: Gif man cuman feormæþ III niht an his agenum hame (cepeman oþþe oðerne þe sio ofer mearce cuman) ⁊ hine þonne his mete fede, ⁊ he þonne ænigum mæn yfel gedo, se man þane oðerne æt rihte gebrenge oþþe riht forewyrce.

Gif man cuman feormæþ III niht an his agenum hame, cepeman oþþe oðerne þe sio ofer mearce cuman, ⁊ hine þonne his mete fede, ⁊ he þonne ænigum mæn yfel gedo, se man þane oðerne æt rihte gebrenge oþþe riht forewyrce.

Gif man cuman feormæþ III niht an his agenum hame, cepeman oþþe oðerne þe sio ofer mearce cumin, ⁊ hine þonne his mete fede, ⁊ he þonne ænignum mæn yfel gedo, se man þane oðerne æt rihte gebrenge oþþe riht forewyrce.

Wenn jemand einen Gast 3 Nächte beherbergt in seiner eigenen Heimstätte (einen Kaufmann oder einen anderen, der über die Grenze hergekommen ist) und ihn ferner mit seiner Speise beköstigt, und der dann einem Menschen Übel zufügt, [so] bringe jener Hausherr den anderen zu Recht[sverantwortung] oder leiste Recht[spflicht] statt [desselben].

If someone gives lodging to a stranger for 3 nights in his own homestead (a merchant or another who has come over the border) and further feeds him with his own food, and the latter then does harm to someone, [then] let that householder bring the other to justice [to answer for it] or perform [the legal duty] in [his] place.

If a man entertains a stranger (a trader or anyone else who has come over the border) for three days in his own home, and then supplies him with food from his own store, and [if] he [the stranger] then does harm to anyone, the man shall bring the other to justice, or make amends on his behalf.

If anyone harbours a stranger, a trader or any other man who has come across the frontier, for three nights in his own home, and then supplies him with his food, and he then does any injury to any man, the man is to bring the other to justice or to discharge the obligations for him.

If a person provides for a visitor for 3 nights in his own home, a merchant or other who has come across the border, and [the host] there feeds him [the guest] his food, and he [the guest] then does harm to any person, that man [the host] should bring the other to justice or do [what is required by] justice for him.

note.seg: Ankömmling, Fremden; s. d. Gl 12a. c; Haftung 7c
Newcomer, stranger; see that word in Gl 12a. c; Haftung 7c

Jedenfalls nicht bloss eines Landguts (wie Price meint, freilich kann auch Gutsgrenze landmeare heissen), sondern mindestens des Gerichtsbezirks; so Toller; vgl. Wi 6. Denn Genossen Einer Gerichtsgemeinde waren leicht belangbar. Auch dachte ein so früher Gesetzgeber wohl noch nicht an Herrschaftsgüter als die normale durchgehende Polizeiorganisation über Freie; vgl. Maitland Domesday 332. Vielleicht ist die Grenze Kents gemeint, der Fremde aber ein Angelsachse. Ein Festländer hiesse wohl ‘Ausländer, über See gekommen’. Auszuschliessen ist ‘Markgenossenschaft’; Stubbs Constit. hist. I 49. 83

In any case not merely of a landed estate (as Price thinks; admittedly an estate boundary can also be called landmeare), but at least of the jurisdictional district; so Toller; cf. Wi 6. For members of one and the same judicial community could easily be sued. Moreover, so early a lawgiver probably did not yet think of lordly estates as the normal, comprehensive police organisation over freemen; cf. Maitland Domesday 332. Perhaps the boundary of Kent is meant, the stranger, however, being an Anglo-Saxon. A man from the Continent would probably be called ‘foreigner, come over the sea’. ‘Mark community’ is to be ruled out; Stubbs Constit. hist. I 49. 83
It is uncertain whether mearc means the frontier of Kent or the border of a district (cf. Wiht. cap. 8).
